Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
List common techniques for acetabular component revision.
Discuss the indications and contraindications for each technique for acetabular component
revision.
Review basic technical aspects for each technique for acetabular component revision.
Describe the complications and outcomes of acetabular component revision.
Indications
Because of an aging population, increasing life expectancy, and expanding indications for
primary total hip arthroplasty, the number of revision total hip arthroplasty procedures is
projected to continue to increase.

The most common reasons for acetabular revision are for the management of dislocation,
mechanical loosening, and implant failure.
Less common indications include periprosthetic fracture, osteolysis, infection, and wear.
Substantial acetabular bone loss may result from osteolysis and stress shielding, further
complicating acetabular revision procedures.
The goal of any acetabular revision procedure is to achieve a durable, stable implant that is
well fixed to the remaining host acetabular bone and oriented to minimize the risk of
dislocation and closely re-create native hip kinematics.
The factors that have the greatest influence on implant durability and stability are the method
of fixation, the biologic potential of surrounding bone, and the inherent stability of the
implant.
Fixation Options
Fixation options include biologic and nonbiologic methods.
Biologic fixation methods rely on interdigitating ingrowth from the surrounding bone to create
secure fixation at the bone-implant interface.
Various implants use biologic fixation, including hemispheric noncemented cups with
anatomic or high hip centers, jumbo cups, oblong cups, or modular noncemented implants.
Nonbiologic fixation methods rely on adjunct fixation to secure the implant to the acetabulum.
Implants that use nonbiologic fixation include cemented polyethylene cups, antiprotrusio
cages, impaction grafts, and total acetabular allografts.
This lesson focuses on biologic noncemented fixation of the revision acetabular component
with the use of augments, cup-cage constructs, and custom triflange implants.
Biologic fixation is the preferred method for acetabular revision.
The biologic potential of the bone immediately surrounding an acetabular implant is crucial to
implant durability.
Successful fixation requires bony apposition and bone viability.
Bony apposition is critical because a gap greater than 150 μm between the implant and bone
prevents bony integration.
The importance of bone viability is demonstrated by evidence suggesting that previously
irradiated bone is associated with early implant failure in noncemented acetabular revision
surgery.
Intraoperative implant stability is a key component of acetabular revision because poor initial
cup fixation is associated with early complications and long-term dysfunction.

The inherent implant-to-bone stability depends on several factors, including bone quality,
accuracy of reaming, and final acetabular component insertion and positioning.
Acetabular cup stability can be increased via supplemental use of additional screws and
augments.
Intraoperative assessment of the degree of bone loss is important to help the surgeon
determine necessary strategies to achieve noncemented biologic fixation.
Preoperative Planning
Preoperative planning is an important step to ensure a safe and efficient procedure and helps
surgeons prepare for contingencies.
Before any revision procedure, the patient should be evaluated for periprosthetic joint
infection.
Copies of the previous implant records may facilitate removal of the acetabular component,
especially if a unique liner locking mechanism requires special tools for removal or if any
atypical screws require a special-shaped screwdriver for removal.
Adequate radiographs, including the entire acetabular implant and enough of the surrounding
pelvic bone, are required to template acetabular reconstruction.
Cross-table lateral radiographs may aid in visualization of the remaining posterior column
bone.
Judet views may aid in identification of bone defects and existing implants.
CT may help quantify the extent of bone loss in patients with massive osteolysis and
questionable discontinuity.
Increased use of three-dimensional (3D) CT software and the ease and affordability of 3D
printing of pelvic models may aid in preoperative planning, especially in patients with massive
bone loss and pelvic discontinuity, which may aid in deciding between cup-cage constructs and
custom triflange implants.
In patients with acetabular protrusion, CT angiography should be considered, and a
preoperative consultation with a vascular surgeon or having a vascular surgeon on backup
during surgery may be necessary.
Preoperative communication with the hospital resource manager and implant vendors is
important to ensure availability of the necessary instrument trays and implants for the
planned surgical procedure and to have additional backup instruments/implants should
intraoperative issues arise.

Potential additional resources to have available for acetabular revision include acetabular
extraction instruments, a universal screw removal tray, a broken screw removal tray, a high-
speed burr, and bone graft options.
Intraoperative fluoroscopy may aid in evaluation of acetabular component orientation and
screw placement to avoid postoperative complications.
Classification
Systematic preoperative interpretation of radiographs may help predict intraoperative stability
and postoperative durability of a revision construct.
Many classification systems have been proposed to aid in this prediction; however, the
Paprosky classification of acetabular bone loss is most commonly used (Table 1; Resource 1).

Reproduced from Sporer SM, Rosenthal BD, Boody BS: Noncemented acetabular revision, in
Lieberman JR, Berry DJ, eds: Advanced Reconstruction: Hip, ed 2. Rosemont, IL, American
Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2017, pp 469-479.
This classification system helps identify inherent stability and the potential for biologic fixation,
which are crucial to implant durability and long-term stability.
The Paprosky classification is based on the severity of bone loss and the ability to attain
noncemented fixation given the pattern of bone loss.
In type I defects, the remaining acetabular bone is completely supportive of a revision implant.
In type II defects, the remaining acetabular bone is partially supportive.
In type III and type IV defects, the remaining acetabular bone is not supportive.
To determine the type of bone defect, the Paprosky classification uses four radiographic
parameters: superior migration of the hip center, ischial osteolysis, teardrop osteolysis, and
the position of the implant relative to the Köhler line.
Superior migration of the hip center refers to bone loss in the acetabular dome, which
consists of bone stock from the anterior and posterior columns. Superior migration is
measured relative to the superior obturator line.
Superomedial migration suggests greater anterior column bone loss, whereas superolateral
migration suggests greater posterior column bone loss.
Ischial osteolysis is bone loss from the inferior aspect of the posterior column and the
posterior wall.
Teardrop osteolysis and disruption of the Köhler line suggest medial acetabular bone loss.
The goal of acetabular reconstruction in patients with a type IIIA defect is to restore full
inherent stability intraoperatively so that a noncemented implant can be used. The shape of a
type IIIA defect is critical in determining the appropriate treatment option.
Spherical defects, which are less common than oblong defects, can be managed with the use
of a jumbo hemispheric cup, with excellent results.
Oblong defects can be managed with the use of a noncemented hemispheric cup with metal
augments.
Bilobed implants are not recommended in for reconstruction because they are associated
with a high rate of loosening and increased technical difficulties.
In oblong type IIIA defects, reconstruction of the acetabulum with a high hip center should be
avoided because a superior shift of the hip center biomechanically affects joint kinematics,
with alterations in abductor muscle exertion required to maintain pelvic stabilization. The use
of a high hip center increases the risk of limb-length discrepancy, dislocation, and altered
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:05 AM
AAOS | Acetabular Component Revision
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000506
5/34

abductor muscle tensioning. In addition, the nonanatomic location of the hip center increases
the risk of impingement.
Another option for the management of oblong type IIIA defects involves the use of a structural
autograft or allograft or metal augmentation to support the porous metal cup.
Several advantages are associated with metal augmentation over allograft.
Metal augments are non-resorbable, which historically has been an issue with allograft used
for pelvic acetabular defects.
Metal augments are technically easier to use, and implant companies currently offer a
greater assortment of shapes and sizes to accommodate variability in defect size and
location.
Metal augments are not associated with a risk of disease transmission.
Metal augments compared with other options do not require extensive stripping of the ilium
or mobilization of the abductors.
Metal augmentation is associated with low rates of loosening, acceptable functional
improvements, and pain relief at a mean follow-up of 5 years.
Paprosky type IIIB defects require substantial additional measures to prepare the defect for a
noncemented acetabular revision component.
If the patient does not have pelvic discontinuity, biologic fixation can be attained with the use
of porous metal augmentation or custom triflange implants.
Patients with acute pelvic discontinuity generally are treated via initial stability with
compression of the posterior column.
Patients with chronic pelvic discontinuity generally are treated via distraction techniques and
a jumbo cup.
The use of a cup-cage construct is another strategy for the management of pelvic
discontinuity. Midterm studies demonstrate good longevity, with the authors of one study on
cup-cage reconstruction reporting survival rates of 93% and 85% at 5 years and 10 years
postoperatively, respectively, with failure defined as revision for any cause.1
Algorithmic Approach
An algorithmic approach to noncemented revision of the acetabular implant is shown in
Figure 1.

Figure 1 Algorithm shows the decision-making process for noncemented acetabular implant
revision. (Reproduced from Sporer SM, Rosenthal BD, Boody BS: Noncemented acetabular
revision, in Lieberman JR, Berry DJ, eds Advanced Reconstruction: Hip, ed 2. Rosemont, IL,
American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2017, pp 469-479.)
The first decision point is assessment of bone stock as indicated by the location of the hip
center.
If the hip center has not migrated more than 3 cm, a trial implant can be inserted to assess
inherent stability. If the remaining bone stock is adequate and provides press-fit stability of
the trial implant, the defect is Paprosky type I or type II, and noncemented fixation of a
hemispheric cup likely will be adequate.
If disruption of the Köhler line is present on radiographs, the defect is type IIC, which will
require rim fixation to support the noncemented hemispheric implant. Medial cancellous
allograft may be useful to lateralize the hip center.
If the hip center has migrated more than 3 cm superiorly or if the trial implant does not have
full press-fit inherent stability, the defect is Paprosky type III.
If partial inherent stability is present, the potential for durable biologic fixation exists, and
the defect is graded type IIIA.
The shape of the defect dictates the necessary revision implant options.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:05 AM

7/34

In patients with a spherical type IIIA defect, a jumbo hemispheric cup may be beneficial.
Oblong defects can be managed with the use of a hemispheric cup with a high hip center,
a hemispheric cup with a modular porous metal augment, or a hemispheric cup with
allograft (fallen out of favor compared with metal augmentation).
If the trial implant demonstrates no inherent stability, the defect is graded type IIIB.
In these patients, pelvic discontinuity should be assessed intraoperatively by compressing
the anterior and posterior columns with the use of a Cobb elevator and assessing the
motion between the superior and inferior hemipelves.
If no pelvic discontinuity exists, treatment options include nonbiologic fixation with
impaction allograft and a cage, nonbiologic fixation with structural allograft and a cage,
biologic fixation with modular porous metal augmentation, and biologic fixation with the
use of a custom triflange implant.
If pelvic discontinuity is observed intraoperatively, the potential of the discontinuity to
heal must be determined. If the discontinuity appears to have healing potential, it is
considered acute; if the discontinuity does not appear to have healing potential, it is
considered chronic.
Acute pelvic discontinuities are managed via compression plating in addition to one of
the aforementioned options for the management of type IIIB defects.
Chronic pelvic discontinuities are managed via distraction with the insertion of bone
graft into the defect, which enhances initial stability. The distracted defect subsequently
is managed with the use of an acetabular cup and cage, a porous metal implant with a
porous metal augment, or a custom triflange implant.
Surgical Setup and Exposure
An extensile exposure is used to facilitate extraction of the implant. Ideally, exposure should
be an extension of previous incisions to avoid skin bridges and flap necrosis.
For the posterior approach, the plane between the iliotibial band and the underlying vastus
lateralis may be difficult to redevelop because of scarring; extending the incision distally may
facilitate easier exposure to find the plane.
Dissection is carried down to the short external rotators and the posterior capsular tissues, if
they are present and identifiable, and a posterior flap is created subperiosteally from the
greater trochanter to the superior aspect of the acetabulum and extended distally along the
proximal femur as necessary for visualization of the joint.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:05 AM
AAOS | Acetabular Component Revision
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000506
8/34

Subperiosteal dissection of the posterior column and the superior aspect of the ilium is
performed to improve exposure.
The femur is retracted anteriorly to allow for complete exposure of acetabular hardware. If
the femoral implant will be retained, superoanterior capsulotomy and débridement of any
dense scar tissue may be necessary to create a pocket for the trunnion to adequately allow
the femoral stem and bone to be translated anteriorly to allow for better visualization of the
acetabulum.
After the liner and acetabular fixation screws are removed, the previous acetabular shell is
extracted, with the goal of performing this step in a meticulous fashion to minimize bone
loss, which may compromise revision implant fixation.
Removal of well-fixed noncemented implants is particularly challenging because of the high
risk of bone loss. Techniques to minimize bone loss include the use of curved osteotomes,
the use of pneumatic impact wrenches, keyhole osteotomies, the use reciprocating saws,
and the use of metal-cutting burrs.
The authors of this lesson prefer to use an acetabular implant removal device. The device
consists of a blade that is attached to a handle with a headpiece that fits into the liner. The
blades (short and long) match the outer diameter of the acetabular shell. The center of
rotation is maintained with the use of a headpiece that matches the inner diameter of the
acetabular shell. The first blade is shorter and used to disrupt the dense peripheral bone and
open a passage for the second blade, which is longer and equal in length to the radius of the
cup. The second blade functionally frees the dome of the acetabular shell. This technique
causes minimal bone loss, allows for time-efficient implant removal, and poses minimal risk.
Final assessment of remaining acetabular bone stock may guide acetabular reconstruction
options. Systematic débridement of any interface membrane and granulation tissue
improves visualization of the remaining bone stock and allows for assessment of pelvic
discontinuity.
Paprosky type I defects
A hemispheric, noncemented implant likely will have full inherent stability in patients with a
type I defect.
The level of the true acetabulum is determined by placing a retractor in the obturator
foramen, which is at the level of the inferior border of the acetabulum.
Acetabular reaming is performed with the use of sequentially larger hemispheric reamers
until the anterior and posterior columns are engaged. In general, sacrifice of anterior
acetabular bone poses less risk for accidental pelvic discontinuity than reaming of posterior
acetabular bone.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:05 AM
AAOS | Acetabular Component Revision
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000506
9/34

If the prosthesis is implanted in 45° of abduction and 15° of anteversion, it may be partially
uncovered. As much as 25% to 30% of incomplete coverage should be tolerated, and the
surgeon should resist the temptation to place the implant more vertically to improve implant
coverage. Substantial deviation from these measures may increase the risk of dislocation and
wear.
Cavitary defects may be packed with local autograft or allograft via impaction grafting
techniques and then by reverse reaming the acetabulum 2 mm smaller than the largest
reamer that was used.
Press-fit fixation can be attained if the periphery of the implant is 2 mm larger than the
largest hemispheric reamer that was used.
The use of multiple cancellous screws for supplemental fixation is recommended to reduce
micromotion and promote bone ingrowth. No optimal number of screws has been reported,
and the number varies depending on the quality of the initial implant-to-bone press-fit and
the location of any acetabular defects. In general, more screws are better, and screws should
be placed strategically around the cup to ensure solid fixation. A wide spread of the screws,
especially on the inferior half of the acetabular cup, can help reduce micromotion and avoid
cup spinout.
Surgeons should understand the neurovascular structures at risk in each quadrant and use
safe drilling techniques to avoid drilling too deep beyond the bone and avoid injuring the
surrounding soft-tissue structures. Surgeons should have a similar understanding when
using a depth gauge, avoiding passage too deep into the drill hole that may injure
surrounding soft-tissue structures.
Paprosky type IIA defects
Aside from the increased potential need for allograft to fill a cavitary defect, acetabular
reconstruction of type IIA defects is similar to that of type I defects.
A hemispheric noncemented implant is used.
Paprosky type IIB defects
A hemispheric noncemented implant can be used successfully in most patients with a type
IIB defect.
Reconstructions of most type IIB defects is successful without grafting the segmental defect.
Reaming is performed until the anterior and posterior columns are engaged to allow for
intrinsic stability of the trial implant. Acetabular reaming may be slightly superior to improve
coverage of the implant.
As much as 25% to 30% of the superior portion of the acetabular implant can be left
uncovered without the need for supplemental support.

Cavitary defects may be packed with local autograft or allograft via impaction grafting
techniques and then by reverse reaming the acetabulum 2 mm smaller than the largest
reamer that was used.
Press-fit fixation can be attained if the periphery of the implant is 2 mm larger than the
largest hemispheric reamer that was used.
The use of multiple cancellous screws for supplemental fixation is recommended to reduce
micromotion and promote bone ingrowth. No optimal number of screws has been reported,
and the number varies depending on the quality of the initial implant-to-bone press-fit and
the location of acetabular defects. In general, more screws are better, and screws should be
placed strategically around the cup to ensure solid fixation. A wide spread of the screws,
especially on the inferior half of the acetabular cup, may help reduce micromotion and avoid
cup spinout.
Surgeons should understand the neurovascular structures at risk in each quadrant and use
safe drilling techniques to avoid drilling too deep beyond the bone to avoid injuring the
surrounding soft-tissue structures. Surgeon should have a similar understanding when using
a depth gauge, avoiding passage too deep into the drill hole that may injure surrounding
soft-tissue structures.
Paprosky type IIC defects
A hemispheric noncemented implant can be used in patients with a type IIC defect.
Reaming is performed until the anterior and posterior columns are engaged to allow for
intrinsic stability of the trial implant. The acetabular reamer may be advanced too deep if the
surgeon does not recognize the false depth of the defect medially. To avoid this situation, the
reamers should contact only the rim of the acetabulum and avoid advancing to the false
medial wall/membrane, which may increase the size of the medial defect and compromise
remaining bone stock.
After the reamer attains adequate fit between the anterior and posterior columns, a medial
defect will be present. The medial defect is filled via impaction grafting with the use of
allograft particulate bone. In some patients, these defects may be very large, and as many as
two femoral heads with a bone mill may be necessary to completely fill the defect. Surgeons
must communicate with the operating room management team in advance to have the
appropriate amount of bone graft available for these types of revision procedures.
If the remaining medial wall is insufficient to buttress the bone graft, a wafer of femoral head
allograft with a diameter greater than that of the defect can be used as a buttress. Similarly,
some commercially available porous metal wafers also can be used as a medial buttress
before impacting the particulate bone graft into the medial defect.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:05 AM

11/34

The key to ensuring proper lateralization of the acetabular shell is to respect the anterior and
posterior wall locations during acetabular component placement to ensure that the edges of
the shell are prominent or flush with the anterior and posterior wall. If the acetabular
component is recessed under the edges of the anterior or posterior column, the component
likely is too medial from the desired hip center.
The acetabular implant is placed with 2-mm press-fit fixation. If the acetabulum is between
cup sizes, the larger cup size is used. A cup with multiple holes is used.
The use of multiple cancellous screws for supplemental fixation is necessary in type IIC
defects to reduce micromotion and promote bone ingrowth. No optimal number of screws
has been reported, and the number varies depending on the location of remaining host bone
for screw fixation because the size of the medial defect may vary and the newly impacted
bone graft will not have adequate stability for screw fixation to support the new acetabular
component. In general, more screws are better, and screws should be placed strategically
around the cup to ensure solid fixation. A wide spread of the screws, especially on the
inferior half of the acetabular cup, may help reduce micromotion and avoid cup spinout.
Surgeons should understand the neurovascular structures at risk in each quadrant and use
safe drilling techniques to avoid drilling too deep beyond the bone and avoid injuring the
surrounding soft-tissue structures. Surgeons should have a similar understanding when
using a depth gauge, avoiding passage too deep into the drill hole that may injure
surrounding soft-tissue structures.
Paprosky type IIIA defects
The shape of a type IIIA defect is critical in determining the appropriate treatment option.
Spherical defects can be managed with the use of a jumbo hemispheric cup.
Options for the management of oblong defects are a noncemented hemispheric cup with
high hip center, a noncemented hemispheric cup, or a porous metal cup with superior metal
augmentation (Figure 2).

radiograph demonstrates acetabular reconstruction with the use of a jumbo cup and a hemi-
augment superomedially to help bring down the hip center and fill the cavitary defect to
support the cup. (Courtesy of Ryan M. Nunley, MD, Creve Coeur, MO, and Charles M. Lawrie,
MD, St Louis, MO.)
Bilobed implants are not recommended because they are associated with a high rate of
loosening and increased technical difficulties.
The authors of this lesson prefer not to use a hemispheric cup with a high hip center because
of the risk for impingement and other potential complications.
After exposure of the acetabulum, the native hip center is identified via the cotyloid notch or
the transverse acetabular ligament.
Progressive reaming is performed in an anatomic position with the use of sequentially larger
reamers until the anterior and posterior columns are engaged to allow for intrinsic stability
of the trial acetabular implant.
With the trial implant in place (with appropriate version and abduction), the superior
augment is placed. Metal augments can be placed in any position and orientation to improve
initial stability. A barrel burr can be used on the augment or the host bone to optimize the
contact area between the two surfaces. A gap of 1 to 2 mm is left between the cup and the
augment for placement of cement.
With the trial acetabular implant in place, some surgeons prefer to place the final augment
before the final acetabular component. In this workflow, the final augment is fixed with the
use of screws, and the augment can be packed with the use of bone graft if necessary. The
portion of the metal augment directly facing the cup should remain free of any debris (eg,
bone graft, soft tissue) to allow for polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) cement to interface in
the next step.
Several options are available for the application of the PMMA cement, and the use of
antibiotic-laden cement should be considered. An attempt should be made to place screws in
the revision cup before the cement hardens to eliminate motion during final seating of the
screws.
Some surgeons prefer to place the PMMA cement onto the revision cup only in areas that
will be in contact with the augment before insertion. The challenge with this technique is
that it requires careful placement of the cement onto the acetabular implant and careful
retraction of the soft tissues to avoid cement migration onto the surface of the cup that is
needed for contact with the limited remaining host bone.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:05 AM
AAOS | Acetabular Component Revision
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000506
14/34

Some surgeons prefer to wait and place the PMMA cement onto the augment and fill the
gap between the augment and the acetabular component after the final cup has been
impacted and the cup screws have been placed. The challenge with this technique is that
application of the cement after the final cup and augment have been placed may be messy
and introduction of sufficient cement into the augment-cup interface may be difficult.
Some surgeons prefer an alternative workflow, with placement of the final acetabular
component and screws before placement of the final metal augment. Advantages and
disadvantages are associated with both workflows, and the choice between the two options
may vary based on surgeon preference/comfort with the techniques, the size/location of the
acetabular defect, and the initial stability of the acetabular construct before supplementation
of the augment.
Paprosky type IIIB defects
Type IIIB defects require substantial measures to achieve noncemented acetabular revision
reconstruction.
Type IIIB defects without pelvic discontinuity
In patients with a type IIIB defect without pelvic discontinuity, nonbiologic augments are
used to reconstruct the pelvis.
All margins of the acetabular defect must be exposed.
Progressive reaming is performed until two points of fixation (anterior-posterior, anterior-
inferior, posterior-inferior) can be achieved.
The inferior bone stock (ischium) often is minimally involved.
A trial implant is placed. Intrinsic stability is not possible.
Augments are placed to decrease acetabular volume and facilitate press-fit fixation
between the cup and the augment. Attempts are made to place the augment in direct
contact with the revision cup. The augment is secured.
With the augment in place, reverse reaming is performed to pack the augment with bone
graft.
Next, the bone graft is cleared from the exposed host bone to maximize contact between
the host bone and the porous revision cup.
The cup is placed. An attempt is made to place screws inferiorly into the ischium to avoid
cup pullout. A manual assessment of the acetabular construct should be performed at
the end of the procedure to ensure that adequate stability is present to avoid excessive
micromotion, which may compromise sufficient host bone interdigitation and long-term
biologic fixation.
Type IIIB defects with chronic pelvic discontinuity
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:05 AM
AAOS | Acetabular Component Revision
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000506
15/34

In patients with a type IIIB defect and chronic pelvic discontinuity, a porous acetabular
implant is used to reconstruct the pelvis with internal biologic fixation.
All margins of the acetabular defect and the discontinuity are thoroughly exposed.
If gross motion is observed and bone contact is possible, a posterior column plate is used.
Progressive reaming is performed until two points of fixation (ie, anterior-posterior,
anterior-inferior, posterior-inferior) are achieved.
A trial implant is placed. Intrinsic stability is not possible.
Augments are used to decrease the acetabular volume and facilitate press-fit fixation
between the cup and the augment. Attempts are made to place the augment in direct
contact with the revision cup.
The discontinuity is bridged with the use of the augment. Screws are placed cephalad and
caudal.
Fibrous tissue is removed from the discontinuity. The cancellous allograft is placed.
With the augment in place, reverse reaming is performed to pack the augment with bone
graft.
Bone graft is cleared from the exposed host bone to maximize contact between the host
bone and the revision cup.
The cup is placed and secured with the use of multiple screws. A manual assessment of
the acetabular construct should be performed at the end of the procedure to ensure
adequate stability and avoid excessive micromotion, which may compromise sufficient
host bone interdigitation and long-term biologic fixation.
Alternatively, an emerging strategy for the management of pelvic discontinuity involves
the use of a cup-cage construct (Figure 3). In this method, a porous-coated shell is placed
via a standard press-fit technique. Screw fixation is used to augment the press-fit stability.
An antiprotrusio cage is cemented within the shell. Screw fixation of the cage to the
ischium and ilium is achieved. Finally, a polyethylene liner is cemented into the cage in the
desired orientation.

The surgical procedures described in this lesson vary. The postoperative protocol is
individualized based on the severity of the defect, the method of fixation, and other medical
comorbidities.
Noncemented acetabular revision often is complicated by bone loss, which compromises
implant fixation and stability. Regardless, a noncemented hemispheric implant can be used
successfully in most acetabular revision procedures. By following the algorithm presented in
this lesson, surgeons can systematically address complex patterns of bone loss and attain
stable intraoperative fixation, even in patients with severe bone loss.
The primary indication for the use of porous metal augments during acetabular revision
surgery is to address any associated bone defect about an unstable acetabular component to
augment cup stability for biologic fixation and to help position the hemispheric acetabular
implant at the correct anatomic level. Metal augments can be used to address contained or
uncontained bone defects.

The primary indication for the use of a custom triflange acetabular cup is massive acetabular
bone loss (typically with Paprosky type IIIB) that precludes the ability to attain a stable
construct with the use of a standard hemispheric revision implant (Figure 4).
Figure 4 AP radiographs of a pelvis. A, Preoperative radiograph demonstrates failed right
complex revision total hip arthroplasty with substantial bone loss and superior femoral
implant migration. B, Postoperative radiograph demonstrates placement of a custom triflange
acetabular cup and a hemi-augment between the triflange and the remaining superomedial
host bone. (Courtesy of Ryan M. Nunley, MD, Creve Coeur, MO, and Charles M. Lawrie, MD, St
Louis, MO.)
Patients with a massive acetabular bone defect typically have undergone multiple previous
surgical procedures. Therefore, infection must be ruled out preoperatively in all patients in
whom a custom triflange implant is being considered. The infection workup should include a
complete blood cell count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein level, and
possibly fluoroscopically guided hip aspiration.
Absolute contraindications to the use of a custom triflange implant are persistent infection
and the inability to attain adequate prosthetic fixation because of severe acetabular bone
deficiency.
The decision to use a custom triflange implant must be made well in advance of the surgical
procedure because several weeks are required for the implant to be designed and
manufactured.
Plain radiographs should be obtained to assess bone defects and may include oblique/Judet
pelvic views.
Thin-slice CT scans are essential to evaluate bone loss and assess for pelvic discontinuity.

3D CT reconstruction images and the use of rapid prototyping technology are necessary to
design and produce the custom triflange implant.
An acrylic model of the hemipelvis or the entire pelvis is created based on the 3D CT
reconstruction images.
The acrylic model is shipped to the surgeon with a provisional plan created by an engineer at
the implant company that shows the proposed cup orientation, hip center, shape and size of
the three flanges, and position of screws for fixation.
The surgeon then reviews the proposed custom triflange construct; in many instances,
multiple modifications are necessary, and extensive communication may be required
between the surgeon and the design engineer. This process may take as long as 4 to 6
weeks.
A custom triflange implant typically requires a very extensile approach, and the authors of this
lesson prefer to use an extensile posterolateral approach; however, an extensile anterolateral
or transtrochanteric approach also may be used.
The patient is placed in the lateral decubitus position.
The patient is draped to allow for as much exposure as possible for this extensile approach.
Identification of the sciatic nerve before posterior dissection is imperative. In some patients,
substantial scarring of the nerve may require neurolysis. If the surgical planes are difficult to
identify, the nerve typically is identified distally or proximally in preparation for neurolysis.
Occasionally, release of the iliopsoas and/or gluteus maximus tendons is necessary to allow
for adequate mobilization of the femoral implant to gain necessary access to the acetabular
region.
The acrylic model of the hemipelvis can be sterilized preoperatively and used intraoperatively
to help the surgeon understand pelvic orientation and as a trial model to assess implant
position and fit.
Acetabular exposure includes removal of the existing acetabular implant, cement, and
membrane to facilitate placement of the custom triflange implant. The pelvis is assessed for
subtle discontinuity via application of traction or rotary torque with the use of bone tenacula
placed on the upper and lower aspects of the acetabulum. Excess bone is carefully removed
in accordance with the preoperative plan to shape the pelvis to accommodate the custom
triflange implant. Typically, this is a very small amount of bone that may be best removed
with the use of a high-speed burr, frequently evaluating the extent of bone removal to avoid
excessive bone loss.
Iliac exposure typically requires 3 to 5 cm of bone to allow for placement of the iliac flange of
the component. A trochanteric slide or trochanteric osteotomy may facilitate exposure of the

ilium and decrease tension on the superior gluteal neurovascular pedicle.
Ischial exposure is best achieved by keeping the hip in extension and the knee flexed to
decrease tension placed on the sciatic nerve. Occasionally, subperiosteal release of the origin
of the hamstring is necessary to facilitate adequate exposure and placement of the ischial
flange.
During implantation of the custom triflange implant, the iliac flange is most commonly placed
first because this method places less tension on the superior gluteal neurovascular pedicle
and it is easier to slide distal to proximal under the muscle fibers of the abductors.
Placement of the iliac flange is facilitated by translating the lower limb proximally with hip
flexion and abduction, which relaxes the abductor musculature.
The knee is flexed, and the hip is extended to relax the posterior soft tissues, facilitating
rotation of the pubic and ischial flanges into position.
The ischial flange is critically assessed for overhang to avoid irritation of the sciatic nerve.
Review of the acrylic model on the hemipelvis as a reference after implantation of the actual
triflange component may help ensure that the fit and position of the implant on the host
bone is similar to that noted in the preoperative plan.
The length and position of the screws can be confirmed preoperatively based on the
preoperative plan.
One or two locking screws are placed in the ischial bone, which typically is weakened and
often is osteolytic. The ischial screws are placed before the iliac screws to avoid superior
migration of the implant.
One or two locking screws are placed in the ilium to allow for provisional fixation.
Additional screws are inserted to complete the fixation.
The custom triflange is assessed for motion. If the implant is placed appropriately, very little
motion should be observed.
An intraoperative AP pelvis radiograph is obtained to ensure adequate positioning of the
implant and assess screw lengths.
Pitfalls and complications
Instability
Instability is the most common complication, and it typically is multifactorial in origin and
associated with an incidence of 3% to 30%. Careful preoperative design of the custom
triflange implant is critical to ensure appropriate cup inclination, anteversion, and hip
center position.
Many patients who require a custom triflange acetabular component have associated
abductor insufficiency secondary to multiple surgical procedures or insufficiency of the

27/34

superior gluteal nerve, trochanteric nonunion, or capsular insufficiency, which may explain
the higher rates of dislocation.
If instability is noted intraoperatively, a thorough assessment is performed to determine
any correctable causes of the instability. Often, larger femoral head diameters, dual
mobility, or constrained polyethylene liners are required.
If the abductor mechanism is intact, trochanteric advancement may be helpful.
Sciatic nerve injury
This occurs in a small percentage of patients. Traction injury is more common than direct
injury to the nerve. The extremity should be positioned with the hip in extension and the
knee in flexion to decrease tension on the nerve during posterior dissection and placement
of the ischial flange.
The ischial flange must be properly designed and positioned to avoid overhang of the
ischium and subsequent irritation of the sciatic nerve.
Careful preoperative assessment is mandatory because the failed acetabular component
may have migrated superiorly and medially, which may cause substantial shortening of the
leg and, therefore, the sciatic nerve. During acetabular reconstruction, restoring the hip
back to the optimal center of rotation in these patients will functionally lengthen the
affected limb and may place the nerve at risk after the hip is reduced to its native position.
In select patients, removal and revision of a well-fixed femoral stem may be necessary to
shorten the femur and achieve an acceptable limb length without excessive nerve tension.
After the trial implants are in place, an intraoperative assessment of sciatic nerve tension
can be performed by manually palpating the nerve while taking the hip from extension and
knee flexion to a straight knee position and flexing the hip. Excessive tension on the nerve
should be addressed before placing the final components.
Mechanical failure of reconstruction
The most common reasons for mechanical problems are failure to attain mechanical
stability of the custom triflange intraoperatively and failure to stabilize a pelvic
discontinuity.
If motion is detected at the time of implantation of the custom triflange, failure is
imminent.
Depending on the specific presentation, various methods can be used to improve implant
fixation during preoperative planning of the custom triflange implant design, including the
use of an increased number of screws, the addition of locking screws, and the application
of hydroxyapatite to the back of the triflange implant.

Intraoperatively, fixation of the custom triflange implant can be customized with cement
augmentation of screws placed into osteolytic/osteoporotic bone, posterior column plating
of pelvic discontinuity, and impaction bone grafting.
A critical characteristic of the implant design is the creation of a central dome that contacts
the remaining ilium superiorly to reduce shear on the flange fixation screws and prevent
additional superior migration of the implant, even in patients with massive acetabular bone
loss or pelvic discontinuity.
Results
Only a handful of case series are available for review because of the rare need for these
custom implants10-16 (Table 3). Short-term and midterm results have been promising, with
reported clinical success rates between 79% and 100%. The complication rates reported in
studies vary. Instability is the most common complication, with an incidence ranging from
zero to 30%. Rates of infection range from zero to 8%. Injury to the superior gluteal and
sciatic nerves also has been described.

A custom triflange cup is a viable solution for acetabular reconstruction in patients with
severe bone loss or pelvic discontinuity. It can be used to achieve a stable construct with rigid
initial implant fixation on the minimal amount of remaining host bone. A custom triflange
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:05 AM
AAOS | Acetabular Component Revision
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000506
30/34

implant accomplishes the major goals of acetabular reconstruction via its ability to
redistribute load anatomically, restore the native hip center, and support osteointegration.
The primary disadvantages of a custom triflange implant is the complexity of understanding
the bone defect and spending the necessary time on the preoperative planning process to
customize the implant design with the engineering team before the implant is manufactured.
The other disadvantage is that 6 to 8 weeks are required to design and manufacture a
custom triflange implant; this may be frustrating for patient with acute acetabular failure
who require complex reconstruction. Advancements in rapid prototyping and 3D printing
likely will reduce this time in the future.
